bib.title: Internet of Agents: Weaving a Web of Heterogeneous Agents for Collaborative Intelligence

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Internet of Agents: Weaving a Web of Heterogeneous Agents for Collaborative Intelligence", Weize Chen, Ziming You, Ran Li, Yitong Guan (equal contribution), Chen Qian, Chenyang Zhao, Cheng Yang, Ruobing Xie, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun (Tsinghua, PKU, BUPT, Tencent). It is arXiv:2407.07061v2 [cs.CL], 10 Jul 2024. The page header reads "Work in progress", and the text names no venue, so treat it as a preprint. The PDF is the v2 text. The code is at github.com/OpenBMB/IoA.

COVERAGE: All 120,498 chars were extracted. I read the main text (abstract through conclusion), the appendices (A.1 message protocol, A.2 client, A.3 server, A.4.1 to A.4.4 experiment details, B, and C.1) and the start of the references. I dropped about 3k chars of embedded LaTeX image blobs ("latexit" lines) from the figure text. The tail of C.2, the nested-team data construction, was only skimmed, as were the later references. The extraction is otherwise clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. Debate loses to single-agent baselines in the paper's own RAG table. Heterogeneous IoA is roughly level with GPT-4 overall. Its gain comes from multi-hop 2WMHQA, and it loses on HotpotQA.
   - number: Overall: GPT-4 0.611; GPT-3.5 alone 0.476; Self Consistency 0.514; Multi-Agent Debate1 (Du) 0.507; Debate2 (Liang) 0.529; Reflexion 0.495; Apollo's Oracle 0.597; IoA 2 agents heterogeneous 0.610; IoA 2 agents homogeneous 0.652; IoA 3 agents homogeneous 0.671.
   - setup: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 core. TriviaQA, NQ, HotpotQA and 2WMHQA. Heterogeneous means each agent has a different evidence pool (Wikipedia or Google). Homogeneous means every agent has both pools. Answers graded by GPT-4 with CoT. Single run, no variance reported.
   - quote: "IoA + 2 Agents (Heterogeneous) 0.803 0.708 0.478 0.449 0.610" and "IoA + 2 Agents (Homogeneous) 0.820 0.671 0.586 0.530 0.652" and "IoA + 3 Agents (Homogeneous) 0.908 0.682 0.575 0.519 0.671"
   - where: Table 3, p.12
   - Caution: the Table 3 caption says IoA "performs on par with or better than GPT-4 across all tasks". The table does not support that. Heterogeneous HotpotQA is 0.478 against GPT-4's 0.566.

2. Adding a third agent does not always help. The paper says optimal agent count is task-dependent.
   - number: none beyond Table 3.
   - setup: homogeneous, 2 vs 3 agents.
   - quote: "the 2-agent homogeneous configuration outperforms the 3-agent setup on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that optimal agent configuration may be task-dependent"
   - where: §3.4, p.12

3. Communication cost: the multi-agent layer's chat costs more than either worker agent, and about half of it was repetition.
   - number: AutoGPT $0.39 standalone, $0.33 in IoA. Open Interpreter $0.16 standalone, $0.13 in IoA. IoA communication $0.53, or $0.28 deduplicated. IoA overall $0.99, or $0.74 deduplicated.
   - setup: 153-task open-ended benchmark, GPT-4-1106-preview. The deduplication was done manually by the authors, by removing repetitions and recounting tokens.
   - quote: "the IoA introduces an additional communication cost of $0.53 per task, resulting in an overall cost of $0.99." and "this resulted in a nearly 50% reduction in communication costs"
   - where: §4.2, Table 5, p.13

4. Failure mode: agents restate and rephrase earlier messages, mostly after several async task assignments. They often fail to switch to the pause & trigger state even though it is available. The authors say this appears in other multi-agent work (Li et al., 2023; Mandi et al., 2023).
   - number: none.
   - quote: "modern LLMs are well-aligned to be effective chatbot assistants, they may not be optimally aligned to be efficient communicating agents."
   - where: §4.2, p.13-14

5. Win rates against standalone agents, judged by an LLM.
   - number: overall 76.5% win vs AutoGPT and 63.4% vs Open Interpreter. Per-category figures are in Fig. 5, with tie and lose shares.
   - setup: 153 open-ended instructions (52 search & report, 30 coding, 30 math, 41 life assistance). Judge is GPT-4-1106-preview. Response order is swapped, and a win counts only if the same system wins in both orders; otherwise it is a draw. IoA integrates AutoGPT and Open Interpreter.
   - quote: "Overall, IoA achieves a remarkable win rate of 76.5% against AutoGPT and 63.4% against Open Interpreter."
   - where: §3.2, p.10, Fig. 5, App. A.4.2
   - Caution: the Introduction says "a 66 to 76% win rate". That does not match the 63.4% result. The benchmark is the authors' own, and the judge is a GPT model.

6. GAIA validation: a team of four basic ReAct agents with one tool each is marginally best overall.
   - number: IoA 40.00 overall against AutoGen 39.39, FRIDAY 34.55, GPT-4+Plugins 14.60, AutoGPT-4 4.85, GPT-4 6.06. Level 1: IoA 50.94 against AutoGen 54.72 (IoA is lower). Levels 2 and 3: IoA 40.70 and 15.38.
   - setup: GPT-4-1106-preview. Agents: web browser, code interpreter, Wikidata searcher, YouTube transcript downloader. Validation set only, "due to budget constraints". Single run.
   - quote: "IoA /users 50.94 40.70 15.38 40.00"
   - where: Table 1, p.9, A.4.1
   - The margin over AutoGen is 0.6 points and no variance is reported.

7. RoCoBench embodied tasks: IoA matches or beats a purpose-built dialog baseline and an oracle central planner on success rate. It needs slightly more steps than Central Plan.
   - number: IoA success Cabinet 1.00, Sweep 0.80, Sandwich 1.00, Sort 1.00, Rope 0.70. Roco Dialog: 0.75, 0.70, 0.70, 0.70, 0.70. Central Plan: 0.90, 1.00, 0.96, 0.70, 0.50. On Sweep, Central Plan (1.00) beats IoA (0.80).
   - setup: 10 runs per task for IoA and Roco Dialog. Central Plan numbers are copied from Mandi et al. (2023). Pack Grocery was omitted because of benchmark implementation errors. Two IoA clients with no integrated agents.
   - quote: "IoA Success 1.00 0.80 1.00 1.00 0.70"
   - where: Table 2, p.11
   - The setup used a new group chat per action for Cabinet and Rope "to optimize costs", and kept history for Sort, Sandwich and Sweep.

8. Nested team formation is argued to cut communication channels. This is a formula, not a measurement.
   - number: full mesh c_full = |g|(|g|-1)/2, versus the sum over sub-groups, which is at most c_full.
   - quote: "cnested = Pgi∈S(g) |gi|(|gi|−1)2 ≤ cfull." (extraction-garbled; it is the sum over sub-groups of |gi|(|gi|-1)/2)
   - where: §2.3.2, p.5

9. Team formation (agent discovery) precision on a simulated, GPT-generated benchmark.
   - number: Regular Top@1 41.4%, Top@10 64.9%, MR 27.4, MRR 50.1%. Nested Top@1 59.7%, Top@10 81.8%, MR 10.6, MRR 66.5%.
   - setup: 625 GPT-4-generated tasks paired with 1500 dummy agent profiles. Top@10 counts an agent as recalled if a recruited agent is among the 10 most similar to a labeled agent, so it is a semantic-similarity measure and not an exact match.
   - quote: "Regular 41.4% 64.9% 27.4 50.1%" and "Nested 59.7% 81.8% 10.6 66.5%"
   - where: Table 4, p.13
   - The regular and nested settings use different datasets, so the two rows are not directly comparable.

10. Design: the group chat is a five-state finite-state machine whose transitions and next speaker are chosen by an LLM.
    - setup: the states are discussion, sync task assignment, async task assignment, pause & trigger, and conclusion. Only one agent speaks at a time. Task assignment and the speaker choice are made by the LLM, with state constraints.
    - quote: "S = {sd, ss, sa, sp, sc} is the set of states representing discussion, synchronous task assignment, asynchronous task assignment, pause & trigger, and conclusion, respectively."
    - where: §2.3.3, p.6

11. The integration protocol is minimal. A third-party agent needs one function. Loop and depth guards are built in.
    - quote: "requires agents to implement a function def run(task desc: str) -> str , which accepts a task description as input and returns a summary of the task completion."
    - quote: "To prevent infinite loops, IoA imposes a limit on the maximum number of tool calls, set to 10 by default."
    - quote: "max turns (int): The maximum number of discussion turns allowed for the current group chat. If exceeded, the group chat will be forced into the conclusion phase."
    - where: A.2.1, A.2.3, A.1 (pp.20-22)
    - Related protocol fields: team_up_depth caps nested team depth, and the header carries sender, state and comm_id.

12. Discovery uses a registry of natural-language agent descriptions searched by embedding or BM25. Server: Milvus vector DB. Client: SQLite and WebSocket.
    - where: §2.3.1, A.3.1, A.3.3

LIMITS
- Authors concede the cost overhead and the repetitive communication. They say prompt optimization and protocol refinement should reduce it, but they did not test that.
- The Security Module is "not extensively utilized in the current implementation" (A.3.1). Authentication, load balancing and fault tolerance are described as future work. Despite the "Internet" framing, nothing in the experiments tests malicious or untrusted agents.
- Experiments are single-run except RoCoBench (10 runs). No confidence intervals are given. GAIA used the validation set only. LLM-as-judge was used on the authors' own benchmark. The team-formation benchmark is synthetic.
- The abstract says IoA outperforms baselines "consistently", but the tables show exceptions: GAIA Level 1 against AutoGen, HotpotQA against GPT-4, and Sweep against Central Plan.
- The paper reports no experiment of IoA against one strong agent with matched cost, and no ablation of the FSM or nested teams. Only the cost analysis (Table 5) compares IoA with standalone agents.
- Inconsistency: the RAG setup says "250 randomly sampled" per dataset, but A.4.4 says "randomly sample 500 entries". The two sample sizes conflict.
- It uses 2023 to 2024 models (GPT-4-1106-preview, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125), so the results are dated.

BUILDS ON: AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), AgentVerse (Chen et al., 2023), MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023), ChatDev (Qian et al., 2023a). Speech Act Theory (Austin 1975; Searle 1969, 1976) and agent communication languages (Finin et al. 1994, KQML; Labrou et al. 1999). Coalition formation (Rahwan et al. 2009). Service discovery (Meshkova et al. 2008). Layered architecture (Bass et al. 1999). ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) agents. Multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2023). Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023). Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023d). Apollo's Oracle (Wang et al., 2023b) for the RAG setup. RoCoBench and Roco Dialog (Mandi et al., 2023). GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023). Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2023e) and MT-Bench pairwise judging (Zheng et al., 2023a, b) for the open-ended benchmark. Finite-state-machine use in agents (Liu & Shuai 2023; Wu et al. 2024a; Li et al. 2024).

CODE: none worth keeping. The protocol signatures are the useful part:
- `search_agent(desc: list[str]) -> list[agent]` and `launch_group_chat(team_members: list[str] | None) -> comm_id` (A.2.3, p.22)
- `def run(task_desc: str) -> str` (A.2.1, p.21)

FIGURES (captions only, from the text):
- Fig. 1, p.3: conceptual layered architecture of client and server. It is useful for seeing the registry, session, routing and security blocks.
- Fig. 2, p.5: nested team formation example, with group chats that spawn sub-group chats. It is the fastest way to see how channels are cut.
- Fig. 3, p.6: the group-chat state transitions. It is the picture to cite next to the AutoGen speaker-transition table.
- Fig. 4, p.8: walkthrough of writing a research paper with sub-group launch.
- Fig. 5, p.10: win, tie and lose bars per category against AutoGPT and Open Interpreter.
- Fig. 6, p.14: an example of repeated, rephrased communication.
- Fig. 7, p.20: fields of the message protocol.

PROBLEMS:
- The PDF carries embedded LaTeX image blobs, which I removed. No instructions were embedded in the text.
- I did not run the figure-captions script. The captions above are from the extracted text.
- The ledger grep for this paper returned nothing relevant. I did not check the target note's `sources:` list for arXiv 2407.07061 beyond reading the note. It is not listed there.
- Relevance to the note (informational): the note's FSM and transition-table material, the cap and stop sections, the "agents spend tokens coordinating" claim (Albada) and the Optima verbosity result are all sharpened by claims 3, 4 and 10. Claims 1 and 2 add a debate-versus-single-agent data point on RAG.
